paragraphs.text: A sermon by John Chrysostom for Holy Thursday. Truly I am distressed, overcome with dread. How shall I satisfy your thirst for hearing? What banquet of words shall I set before you? How shall I entertain so many people, whom Christ alone strives to satisfy? For the joy of the whole world is already at the doors. The calm of the Lord’s resurrection is drawing near. Again the senseless Jewish people are in turmoil. Again the dogs bark at the shepherd. Again the servants plot against their master. Again the workers of darkness take counsel. Again Judas rehearses his lawless betrayal. Again the Jews prepare silver to send into Hades him who is free among the dead. And they will learn that death is [?].

So that the tombs may be shaken and the dead may be given wings to rise again. Again the disciple sells him. And those trained in the law buy him. And the thief on the cross proclaims him God. But let us recall the betrayer’s words. “What are you willing to give me,” he said, “and I will hand him over to you?” What are they willing to give you, foolish Judas? A rope to hang yourself, outer darkness, unquenchable fire, deprivation of the kingdom of God, separation from the saints, a fall from which there is no rising. That was what you gained from the Jews through your bargain. What can they give you that could equal all you stand to lose, you lawless man, full of every evil? Why do you sell so cheaply the Creator of heaven and earth, who carries everything in the palm of his hand? When he saw his Master being honored, and saw costly ointment being poured upon his exalted head, he reproached the woman who honored him and cried out, “Why this waste of ointment? Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor?” So you valued the ointment, prepared from various fragrances and skillfully blended, at three hundred denarii. But the true ointment, whose fragrance raises the dead when they smell it, you sell for thirty pieces of silver. You do not know what you are selling, Judas. The intoxication of greed has blinded you. When have you seen a master sold by his servant? When have you learned to sell

light in order to buy darkness? Why have you scorned the knowledge of love? Why do you carry out your betrayal with a kiss? Was it not rightly that the prophet exposed you, crying out from afar: “His mouth is full of curses, bitterness, and deceit. Under his tongue are trouble and suffering.” Like a sharpened razor, you practiced deceit. You were kissing your own Master. Come forward and kiss him! The patient Master endures you, not turning away from the foul stench of your kiss, but the gift he had given you he was taking out of your mouth. Oh, how evil the love of money is! For because of it the disciple left the ranks of the apostles and took a rope to hang himself, and it showed its fitting power upon the throat through which the words of betrayal had come. But leaving this ungodly man behind, let us turn our discourse to the godly robber. O ineffable light! For through it the robber leaped from the cross into paradise. For when he saw the Lord hanging in the middle, and the whole world shaking with fear, and the sun being covered with terrible sorrow, and the light of day fleeing, and the fabric of creation casting off its order, and the rocks splitting apart—having seen all this and taken it to heart, and not knowing what words to say to his fellow robber [?], and seeing all creation swaying this way and that and trembling, he recognized the one hanging in the middle as the Master of all that trembled. And recognizing him there,

he immediately cried out: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom.” Truly the robber became a worker of the eleventh hour. For he completed the work of the whole day of life. And although he was hired for only one hour, he worked well. He did not grow weary in faith. He paid no attention to blasphemies or wounds; he disregarded the Jews’ insults. Taking the whole world as his teacher and recognizing the Master of the whole world, he offered him fitting worship. What did Christ, the giver of rewards, who loves to honor those who do good, do in return for this? To the robber who had asked for things to come, he revealed this exceedingly great gift in a single hour. When the robber said, “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom,” immediately the Master, Christ, answered, saying: “Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise.” True is the scripture that says: “While you are still speaking, I will say: ‘Here I am.’” To this Christ and our God be glory and worship, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
